4.10 Thyrotoxicosis and Hyperthyroidism

Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical syndrome that results when tissues are exposed to high levels of circulating thyroid hormones. Hyperthyroidism is characterized by the manifestations resulting from overproduction of hormone by the thyroid gland itself (the thyroid gland is synthesizing and secreting excessive quantities of thyroid hormones). The various forms of thyrotoxicosis are listed in Table 4.4 and are discussed individually below.

Table 4.4 Classification of thyrotoxicosis

I. Thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism

• Graves’ disease

• Toxic multinodular goiter

• Toxic adenoma

• Iodine-induced (Jod–Basedow)

• TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma

II. Thyrotoxicosis without hyperthyroidism (not true hyperthyroidism)

• Thyrotoxicosis factitious (iatrogenic or voluntary ingestion of thyroxine or thyroid hormones)

• Subacute thyroiditis

• Thyroiditis with transient thyrotoxicosis (silent, postpartum thyroiditis, and Hashytoxicosis)

• Ectopic thyroid tissue (struma ovarii)

Thyrotoxicosis and Hyperthyroidism

69

4.10.1 Basedow–Graves’ Disease

Graves’ disease is the most common form of thyrotoxicosis. Females are involved about five times more commonly than males. The syndrome consists of one or more of the following features: thyrotoxicosis, diffuse goiter, infiltrative ophthalmopathy, and dermopathy (pretibial myxedema).

4.10.1.1 Etiology and Pathogenesis

It is an autoimmune disease of unknown cause. Note: There is an underlying genetic predisposition (strong familial predisposition), but it is not clear what triggers the acute episode.

• A number of interacting susceptibility genes are thought to play a role in the

development of disease—a complex genetic trait.

• CTLA-4 (cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4) is associated with Graves’ disease

in Caucasian populations. In particular, the CT60 allele has a prevalence of 60% in the general population but is also the allele most highly associated with Graves’ disease. These data emphasize the complex nature of genetic susceptibility and the likely interplay of environmental factors. Some factors (proposed environmental triggers) that may incite the acute episode include psychological stress, pregnancy, particularly the postpartum period, infection, tobacco use, and iodine exposure. In Graves’ disease, T lymphocytes become sensitized to antigens within the thyroid gland and stimulate B lymphocytes to synthesize antibodies to these antigens. One such antibody is directed against the TSH receptor in the thyroid cell membrane (called thyroid-stimulating antibody (TSAb) or TSH-receptor antibody (TRAb)), or thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)), stimulating thyroid gland growth, vascularity, and rate of thyroid hormone production and secretion.

4.10.2 Toxic Adenoma (Plummer’s Disease)

A toxic adenoma (or true follicular adenoma) is a functioning adenoma hypersecreting T3 and T4 and causing hyperthyroidism. These lesions start out as a small autonomously functioning nodule that slowly increases in size to produce excessive quantities of thyroid hormones. This gradually suppresses endogenous TSH secretion, which results in reduced function of the contralateral lobe of the gland. Several somatic mutations in the TSH-receptor gene that lead to constitutive activation of the TSHR in the absence of TSH are thought to explain the pathogenesis of this condition.

70

4

The Thyroid Gland

The typical patient is an older individual (usually >40) who has noted recent growth of a long-standing thyroid nodule. Symptoms of weight loss, weakness, shortness of breath, palpitations, tachycardia, and heat intolerance are noted. The cardiovascular manifestations may be prominent; infiltrative ophthalmopathy or dermopathy are never present. Physical examination reveals a definite nodule on one side, with very little thyroid tissue on the other side.

4.10.3 Toxic Multinodular Goiter

It usually occurs in older patients with long-standing euthyroid multinodular goiter, from which it emerges slowly; the increase in the extent of autonomous function causes the disease to move from the nontoxic to the toxic phase. Somatic mutations in the TSHR gene (very few have G protein mutations), first demonstrated in toxic adenomas, have been demonstrated also in toxic multinodular goiter, and the individual mutations appear to differ from nodule to nodule. Physical examination reveals a multinodular goiter that may be quite large and even extend substernally and manifestations of hyperthyroidism without signs of autoimmunity.

4.10.4 Iodine-Induced Hyperthyroidism

Administration of pharmacologic doses of iodide-containing drugs to subjects with iodine deficiency goiter results in iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (also called the Iod–Basedow phenomenon) and even Graves’ disease. The main causes include amiodarone (contains 37% iodine (≈75 mg iodide/tb)), coronarography, intravenous urogram/pyelogram, and computer tomography (radiographic contrast media). The clinical presentation includes thyrotoxicosis associated with diffuse or multinodular goiter. Low RAIU and high urinary iodine excretion (>several mg/day) confirm that the patient has been exposed to large quantities of iodine. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis: 2% in the United States

• Due to the excess iodine (also called type 1 amiodarone-induced

thyrotoxicosis)

• Due to an amiodarone-induced thyroiditis, with inflammation and release of

stored hormone into the bloodstream (also termed type 2-amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis)

Thyrotoxicosis and Hyperthyroidism

71

4.10.5 TSH-Secreting Pituitary Adenoma

It is rare and characterized by severe hyperthyroidism and large goiters.

4.10.6 Subacute Thyroiditis and Hashitoxicosis

Subacute thyroiditis and silent or painless thyroiditis, postpartum thyroiditis, and hashitoxicosis may present with symptoms of mild to severe thyrotoxicosis following an acute release of T4 and T3 into the circulation. These illnesses can be differentiated from other forms of thyrotoxicosis in that the RAIU is markedly suppressed and the symptoms usually subside spontaneously over a period of weeks or months.

4.10.7 Struma Ovarii

A teratoma of the ovary contains thyroid tissue that becomes hyperactive. Mild features of thyrotoxicosis result, such as weight loss and tachycardia, but there is no evidence of goiter or eye signs. Serum FT4 and T3 are mildly elevated, serum TSH is suppressed, and RAIU over the neck is low. Total body scan reveals uptake of radioiodine in the pelvis, rather than in the neck. The disease is curable by removal of the teratoma.

4.10.8 Manifestations of Hyperthyroidism (All Forms)

The thyroid hormones overproduction has effects on cardiovascular system, central nervous system, gastrointestinal tube, neuromuscular system, lipid, protein and carbohydrate metabolisms, etc. Clinical presentation includes:

1. General manifestations: High basal metabolic rate and sometimes slightly elevated basal body temperature (37–37.5 °C), heat intolerance and sweating,

fatigue, and weakness.

2. Nervous system: Alterations in nervous system function are manifested by:

(a) Emotional lability, nervousness, and irritability.

(b) Insomnia, restlessness, and shortness of attention span.

(c) Fine, rhythmic tremor of the hands, tongue, or slightly closed eyelids.

(d) Hyperkinesia and hyperreflexia (↑ in the speed of muscle contraction and

relaxation).

72

4

The Thyroid Gland

3. Cardiovascular system

Alterations in cardiovascular function in the thyrotoxic patient are partly due to increased circulatory demands that result from the hypermetabolism and the need to dissipate the excess heat produced.

(a) The most common complaints are palpitations that are the result of increased

cardiac output and ↑↑ heart rate.

(b) Tachycardia is almost always present.

(c) Heart sounds are loud and ringing; functional systolic murmurs may also be

heard in different areas of auscultation (mostly at the apex) (these manifestations abate when a normal metabolic state is restored).

(d) Cardiac arrhythmias are almost invariably supraventricular: extrasystoles,

atrial fibrillation, and paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.

(e) Widening of pulse pressure ← (low peripheral vascular resistance → ↓ diastolic pressure and ↑cardiac output leads to ↑ systolic blood pressure).

(f) Hyperkinetic cardiovascular syndrome; congestive (high output) heart

failure.

4. Digestive manifestations

(a) Increased appetite but with weight loss (because of the ↑ basal metabolic

rate).

(b) Thyroid hormones stimulate gut motility: stools are frequently soft, but diarrhea is rare.

(c) Hepatic dysfunction occurs, particularly when thyrotoxicosis is severe.

5. Muscular effects

Muscle weakness and wasting may be noted; although thyroid hormones stimulate the synthesis of many structural proteins, in hyperthyroidism there is an increased protein turnover and loss of muscle tissue or myopathy.

(a) Weakness is most prominent in the proximal muscles of limbs, causing difficulty in climbing stairs (“chair sign”).

6. Endocrine manifestation

(a) ♀: Ovulation may be impaired, menstrual abnormalities: oligomenorrhea

and secondary amenorrhea.

(b) ♂: Erectile dysfunction and gynecomastia.

7. Skin and hair

(a) Warm, moist, and pink skin (←cutaneous vasodilatation and excessive

sweating); the patient blushes readily.

(b) The hair is fine and friable and hair loss may be excessive; the nails are often

soft and friable.

8. Eyes

(a) Retraction of the upper or lower eyelids, or both, evident as the presence of

a rim of sclera between either lid and the limbus, may be seen in all forms of thyrotoxicosis; responsible for the typical stare of the patient.

Thyrotoxicosis and Hyperthyroidism

73

(b) Also common is either lid lag, a phenomenon in which the upper lid lags

behind the globe when the patient is asked to shift the gaze slowly downward, or globe lag, which becomes evident when the eye lags behind the upper lid when the patient looks up.

(c) A fine tremor of the lightly closed lids can often be observed (Rosenbach’s

sign). These ocular manifestations appear to be the result of increased adrenergic activity. Note: It is important to differentiate these ocular manifestations (=class 1 (O) of the Werner’s classification of eye signs in Graves’ disease), which occur in all forms of thyrotoxicosis, from those of infiltrative orbitopathy, which are characteristic of hyperthyroid Graves’ disease. These manifestations will often abate when the thyrotoxicosis is relieved.

4.10.9 Manifestations of Graves’ Disease

Note: This chapter will present manifestations of Graves’ disease that appear in addition to those common to all forms of thyrotoxicosis, presented above.

• In Graves’ disease, the goiter is diffuse and usual symmetrical; the consistency

varies from soft to firm and rubbery; the surface is generally smooth; in severe cases, a thrill may be felt, usually over the upper poles, and a thrill is always accompanied by an audible bruit (the thrills and bruits are caused by the increase blood flow and are usually continuous but sometimes are present only in systole).

• Ophthalmopathy: Irritation in the eyes, excessive tearing that is often made

worse by exposure to air or wind, exophthalmos, periorbital edema, extraocular muscle dysfunction: double vision, photophobia, chemosis, scleral injection, retrobulbar pressure or pain, exposure keratitis, and optic neuropathy. Proptosis: Upper limits of normal according to race: white 20 mm, Asian 18 mm, Black 22 mm (as measured by the Hertel exophthalmometer). Any combination of these symptoms and signs described above suggests ophthalmopathy, which has been classified by Werner in six classes, as set forth in

Table 4.5. The first letters of each class form the mnemonic NO SPECS.

Classes 2–6 represents true infiltrative disease involving orbital muscle and orbital tissues and are specific to Graves’ disease. Clinical Activity Score (CAS) Activity measures based on the classical features of inflammation is the sum of all items present: –– Spontaneous retrobulbar pain –– Pain on attempted up or downgaze –– Redness of the eyelids –– Redness of the conjunctiva –– Swelling of the eyelids

Table 4.5 Werner’s classification of eye changes in Graves’ disease

• Class 0 (N): No signs or symptoms

• Class 1 (O): Only signs, no symptoms (signs limited to upper lid retraction, stare, lid lag, and

globe lag)

• Class 2 (S): Soft tissue involvement: periorbital edema, irritation in the eyes, excessive tearing,

conjunctival congestion or edema (chemosis), enlarged lacrimal glands; proptosis <22 mm

• Class 3 (P): Proptosis ≥22 mm

• Class 4 (E): Extraocular muscle involvement—ophthalmoplegia; patients may complain of

diplopia due to ocular muscle dysfunction caused by either edema during the early active phase or fibrosis during the later phase (→and failure of muscle relaxation, limiting the function of the antagonist muscle). The inferior rectus is the muscle most commonly involved in the infiltrative process. By failing to relax normally, upward gaze limitation is the most common physical finding in patients with eye muscle involvement. The muscle next most commonly involved is the medial rectus, impairing lateral gaze. Another common finding is a convergence defect caused by infiltrative, fibrotic contraction of the medial rectus

• Class 5 (C): Corneal involvement (keratitis) due to inability to close the eyes completely

=lagophthalmos (proptosis >32 mm)

• Class 6 (S): Sight loss (optic nerve involvement) ← likely due to ischemia of the nerve from

compression of the surrounding enlarged extraocular muscles

–– Inflammation of the caruncle and/or plica –– Conjunctival edema A CAS >3/7 indicates active GO. 4.10.9.1 T  he Pathogenesis of Infiltrative Orbitopathy of Graves’ Disease (Thyroid-Associated Ophthalmopathy or Orbitopathy: TAO) Infiltrative orbitopathy precedes, follows or its onset is simultaneous with thyrotoxic manifestations. It is more frequently in women and more severe in men. The TAO is usually bi/unilateral and symmetrical/asymmetrical. The pathogenesis of ophthalmopathy may involve cytotoxic lymphocytes (killer cells) and cytotoxic antibodies sensitized to a common antigen such as the TSH receptor that is found in orbital fibroblasts, orbital muscle, and thyroid tissue. Cytokines from these sensitized lymphocytes may cause activation and proliferation of orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes, resulting in increased amounts of retro-­ orbital fat and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), which are hydrophilic. The extraocular muscle and adipose tissue are swollen by the accumulation in the extracellular matrix of GAGs that are secreted by fibroblasts. This accumulation disrupts and impairs the function of muscle causing diplopia and also leads to proptosis (protrusion) of the globes; proinflammatory cytokines also lead to redness, congestion, and conjunctival and periorbital edema (thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy or orbitopathy). As the disease runs its course and inflammation is reduced, the damaged muscle become fibrosed.

Thyrotoxicosis and Hyperthyroidism

75

For unclear reasons, smoking cigarettes is a potent risk factor for the development of TAO.

 hyroid Dermopathy (Pretibial Myxedema) and Thyroid T Acropachy

The pathogenesis of thyroid dermopathy (pretibial myxedema) and the rare subperiosteal inflammation on the phalanges of the hands and feet (thyroid osteopathy or acropachy) may also involve lymphocyte cytokine stimulation of fibroblasts in these locations. Thyroid dermopathy consists of thickening of the skin, particularly over the lower tibia or on the dorsum of the feet, with a peau d’orange surface (hyperpigmented, nonpitting induration of the skin). It is relatively rare, occurring in about 2–3% of patients with Graves’ disease. It is usually associated with significant ophthalmopathy and with a very high serum titer of TSAb. Graves’ disease can be associated with other diseases such as DM type 1, Addison disease, vitiligo, celiac disease, and myasthenia gravis.

4.10.10 Investigation of Thyrotoxicosis (Fig. 4.3)

1. Hormonal assessment—thyroid function test

The combination of an ↑FT4 and a suppressed TSH makes the diagnosis of hyperthyroidism. Exception: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (central hyperthyroidism) characterized by high TSH and FT4.

2. Thyroid ultrasonography

(a) Graves’ disease—diffuse thyroid hypertrophy, homogenous aspect;

hypoechoic.

(b) Toxic adenoma/toxic multinodular goiter—one nodule/enlarged gland that

is diffusely inhomogeneous with multiple individual nodules.

3. RAIU (radioactive iodine uptake) and radionucleotide thyroid scan

Employed if diagnosis uncertain, but are seldom required.

(a) ↑ RAIU is present in thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism: Graves’ disease,

toxic adenoma, and toxic multinodular goiter.

(b) ↓ RAIU is present in subacute thyroiditis or “silent thyroiditis,” iodine-­

induced hyperthyroidism. Thyroid scintigraphy (123I or 99Technetium scan) appearance:

Fig. 4.3 Investigations useful in the differential diagnosis of hyperthyroidism

(a) In Graves’ disease, radioiodine scan shows an enlarged gland that is usually

rather symmetric with a typically very homogenous distribution of tracer.

(b) Toxic adenoma appears like a “hot” nodule with ↓ or absent function of the

contralateral lobe.

(c) Toxic multinodular goiter is characterized by multiple functioning nodules

in the gland or occasionally an irregular, patchy distribution of radioactive iodine.

4. Thyroid autoantibodies

TSAbs: Positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAbs or TSAbs or TSI) are highly specific to Graves’ disease (human autoimmune thyroid disease).

(a) Useful in patients who present with unilateral or bilateral exophthalmos

without obvious signs or laboratory manifestations of Graves’ disease.

(b) Useful indicator of the degree of disease activity.

(c) The level of TRAbs correlates with the severity of the eye disease.

(d) Also useful in the assessment of cessation of antithyroid drugs (persisting ↑

titers predicts recurrence) and in pregnant women to assess the risk of fetal thyrotoxicosis.

TPO and TG antibodies are usually present in both Graves’ disease and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

5. Others

(a) Glycaemia normal or ↑/impaired glucose tolerance/DM.

(b) ↓ Cholesterol.

(c) Normal/high alkaline phosphatase (ALP).

(d) ECG: Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, and

left ventricle hypertrophy.

6. Ultrasonography, CT, and MRI scan of the orbits: Reveal extraocular muscle

enlargement in most patients with Graves’ disease and this can be useful in cases of diagnostic difficulty.

4.10.11 Complications

(a) Thyrotoxic crisis (“thyroid storm”) is the acute exacerbation of all of the

symptoms and signs of thyrotoxicosis. It’s a life-threatening condition that presents with fever (38–41 °C), flushing and sweating, cardiac arrhythmias, heart failure, diarrhea, vomiting, marked agitation, delirium, and coma.

(b) Thyrotoxic cardiac involvement (cardiothyreosis) includes cardiac arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation), heart failure, and myocardial ischemia.

(c) Thyrotoxic myopathy appears in severe untreated cases when muscle wasting

(proximal) develops out of proportion.

(d) Thyrotoxic osteoporosis.

(e) Diabetes mellitus.

(f) Thyrotoxic hepatopathy (hepatic dysfunction) occurs particularly when thyrotoxicosis is severe. Clinical presentation includes jaundice, hepatomegaly,

high liver enzymes: alanine transaminase (ALT), and aspartate aminotransferase (AST).

4.10.12 Treatment of Hyperthyroidism

Note: Although autoimmune mechanisms are responsible for the syndrome of Graves’ disease, management has been largely directed toward controlling the hyperthyroidism. Objectives

• To induce remission in Graves’ disease.

• Monitor for relapse off treatment on a regular basis.

78

4

The Thyroid Gland

Three good methods are available: antithyroid drug therapy, surgery, and radioactive iodine therapy. In general, the standard policy in Europe is to offer a course of antithyroid drugs (ATDs) first. In the United States, radioiodine is more likely to be offered as first-­ line treatment.

4.10.12.1 Medical Treatment (ATDs)

Mechanisms of action

The ATDs—methimazole, carbimazole, and propylthiouracil (PTU) act by inhibiting TPO-mediated iodination of thyroglobulin to form T4 and T3 within the thyroid gland.

Imidazole Derivates

Thiamazole (Thyrozol) 5 mg/tb Carbimazole 5 mg/tb Methymazole A typical regimen starts with larger doses (30–40 mg dose) of methimazole/thyrozol for 1–2 months; this dose would then be reduced gradually to 5–10 mg for maintenance therapy.

Thiouracil Derivates

Methylthiouracil (50 mg/tb) Propylthiouracil (50 mg/tb) 5 mg of carbimazole is roughly equivalent to 50 mg of propylthiouracil. PTU but not methimazole blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and thus may have advantages when given at high doses in severe thyrotoxicosis. Both drugs may have immunosuppressive effects that may be responsible for the remission from the disease that some patients have after 1–2 years of treatment. PTU should not be used as a first-line agent because of the potential for severe and potentially fatal hepatotoxicity with its use. However, PTU is preferred in pregnant woman in the first trimester because of rare teratogenic effects of methimazole in the fetus (aplasia cutis) and in patients with life-threatening thyrotoxicosis. The laboratory tests of most value in early monitoring the course of therapy are serum FT4 and T3. TSH levels often remain suppressed for many weeks or even months, and hence are not a reliable index of thyroid function early in the course of treatment. Side effects: Rash (can be managed by administering antihistamines), agranulocytosis (represents indication for discontinuing the medication), cholestatic jaundice with thiamazole, hepatocellular toxicity with PTU and acute arthritis with either drug (require the cessation of therapy), and drug-induced hypothyroidism with goiter.

Thyrotoxicosis and Hyperthyroidism

79

4.10.12.2 Surgical Treatment

Indications

(a) Relapsed of Graves’ disease

(b) Very large, compressive glands, and multinodular goiters

(c) Patients who are allergic to or noncompliant with ATD

(d) Patients who refuse radioactive iodine

(e) Documented suspicious or malignant thyroid nodule by FNAC

Total thyroidectomy is now considered the operation of choice because of the risk of relapse with partial thyroidectomy. All such patients go home on T4. The patient is prepared with ATDs until euthyroid (about 6 weeks); in addition, starting 2 weeks before the day of operation, saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI) or Lugol’s solution (3 × 3 drops daily → 3 × 15 drops/day) is added. This regimen will diminish the hyperplasia and hypervascularity of the gland (the gland usually becomes firm) and simplify surgery. Complications of surgery: Hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

4.10.12.3 Radioactive Iodine Therapy

Indications

(a) Definitive treatment of multinodular goiter or adenoma

(b) Relapsed Graves’ disease

(c) Allergy to ATD

(d) Contraindications to surgery

Radioactive iodine may be given immediately in a dosage of 3–10 mCi I. Following the administration of radioactive iodine (which typically is giving orally as a single capsule), the gland will shrink and the patient will usually become euthyroid over a period of 2–6 months.

131

Side Effects

–– Hypothyroidism is the almost inevitable complication of radioactive iodine therapy, affecting >80% of patients. Serum FT4 and TSH levels should be followed every 6–8 weeks, and when hypothyroidism develops, prompt replacement therapy with T4 is instituted. –– Radioiodine can exacerbate eye problems and may even induce mild eye disease in those without eye disease (especially in patients with severe hyperthyroidism, who smoke cigarettes and in those with elevated TRAbs titers); however, potential worsening can be prevented by administration of prednisone 40–60 mg/day

for 1–2 months (gradually tapering the dose) following the radioiodine treatment. –– Rarely: anterior neck pain caused by radiation-induced thyroiditis (1%); transient rise (72 h) in thyroid hormone levels which may exacerbate heart failure, if present. This aspect needs consideration in elderly patients.

Contraindications

1. Pregnant and lactating ♀

2. Severe ophthalmopathy

3. Young children because of the potential risk of thyroid carcinogenesis

4.10.12.4 Other Medical Measures

• Rest

• Beta-adrenergic blocking agents: propranolol 10–40 mg every 6 h or longer-­

acting beta-blockers: metoprolol and atenolol—control many adrenergic symptoms, tachycardia, and hypertension

• Sedatives

• Multivitamins

4.10.13 Treatment of Infiltrative Orbitopathy

4.10.13.1 Medical Treatment of Graves’ Ophthalmopathy

Stop Smoking!!!

1. Symptomatic treatment (useful mainly in mild forms): Dark glasses (for those

with photophobia, sensitivity to wind, or cold air), artificial tears, keeping the patient’s head elevated at night and the administration of diuretics that may help diminish periorbital edema. Selenium may improve symptoms in patients with mild Graves’ ophthalmopathy, as illustrated by the results of a randomized trial of selenium (100 μg twice daily (bd)).

2. Glucocorticoids:

(a) Intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg/week for 6 weeks followed by

250 mg/week for another 6 weeks) in moderate-severe forms or pulse therapy 1 g/day for 3 days in very severe cases (sight-threatening TAO); IV glucocorticoids have the advantage of fewer SE than with high doses of prednisone.
